title: Pilgrimage: Lumbini
hookLine: the garden of the birth in Nepal, with Ashoka's pillar

cards: Near the border of Nepal and India is a garden with a pond, old brick foundations, and trees hung with bright prayer flags that snap in the wind.
Monks walk the brick paths slowly; a family spreads a cloth on the grass by the water. In the middle stands a plain stone pillar, weathered and gray, with lines of very old writing cut into it.
People come from far away to stand next to that pillar for a minute. Then some sit under a tree and say nothing at all. The place is Lumbini, where the story starts.

teach.b: Start with the oldest reason for going. In the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, the Buddha, near the end of his life, tells his attendant Ananda that there are places a person of faith may visit and be moved.
The first is where you can say: here the Tathagata was born. Tathagata is a name the Buddha uses for himself in the texts.
So pilgrimage isn't something later Buddhists invented on their own; in the text, the Buddha points to it himself. Now the garden.
In the Sutta Nipata, an old collection of verses, gods announce the birth of a future Buddha in the Lumbini country, among the Sakyas.

Later tellings fill in the scene: Queen Maya on her way to her family's home, stopping in a garden, reaching up to a branch of a tree, and giving birth standing. Tradition tells that part with great tenderness.
Then the pillar. The emperor Ashoka, who turned toward the Buddha's teaching after a bloody war, set up stone pillars across his lands.
The one at Lumbini, as scholars read its inscription, records that he came here himself and honored the place because the Buddha was born here.

teach.h: A KING CAME TO THIS GARDEN.
teach.b: A king walking into a garden to stand where a baby was born: that's the whole shape of pilgrimage.
Nothing happens at Lumbini that couldn't happen at home. You walk, you arrive, you stand, and you remember. The place doesn't teach.
It helps you remember the one who did.

how: Buddhists from many countries and schools travel to Lumbini in Nepal, where they walk the sacred garden, see Ashoka's pillar and the site honored as the Buddha's birthplace, and sit, chant or meditate there.

o: a journey to a holy place, made to remember
a walk taken only by monks after ordination
a move to a holy land to live there for good

p: hears the Buddha name the places
reaches for a branch in the garden
the king who set up the pillar

s: pilgrimage was a later idea with no root in the texts
in the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, the Buddha himself names places worth visiting.
the Lumbini pillar was set up by the emperor Ashoka
as scholars read it, the inscription records his own visit to honor the birthplace.
in the text, the Buddha speaks of himself as the Tathagata
it is a name he uses for himself in the discourses.

games.q: you're a king who has heard the Buddha's teaching. a garden far away is where he was born. what do you do?
o: go there yourself and mark the place in stone.
build a new garden near your palace instead.
games.why: as scholars read Ashoka's pillar, he went himself and honored the spot. the pillar still stands in the garden.

practice: Close or lower your eyes and picture the garden: grass, a still pond, prayer flags moving, the gray pillar in the sun.
Sit under a tree in your mind and let the thought settle: a child was born here, and that child became a teacher. If your mind wanders to your own day, walk back into the garden.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, made to remember. In the Buddha's own words, the first of the places worth seeing is where he was born. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit Lumbini: the name of the garden country where the texts place the Buddha's birth.

carryVoice: Your line: where he was born. A garden, a pillar, a long road. Until tomorrow.
